passage:
'Kishore, is this yours?' Gurleen held up the drawing from the school exhibition: an old man at a tea stall, every wrinkle shaded.
'Yeah. Didi, it's nothing.'
'Nothing? It won second prize. Papa's showing it to the neighbours.'
'The judges were just being nice. The first-prize one was actually good.'
'The judge wrote "remarkable use of light".'
'Anyone can do light. You just copy what you see.'
'Then why can't I?'
Kishore shrugged. 'You didn't try.'
'I've tried for years. My cows look like dogs.'
He laughed despite himself. 'That was luck. The tea-stall man just sat still for a long time.'
Gurleen sat down on his bed. 'You know what's funny? When you get something wrong, you never call that luck.'
Kishore went quiet and looked at the drawing for a while.

qa.q: What prize did Kishore's drawing win?
qa.a: Kishore's drawing won second prize.

qa.q: Why does Kishore keep saying it was luck or that anyone can do it?
qa.a: Accepting the praise would clash with Kishore's low view of himself, so explaining it away keeps that view safe, even though it also stops him enjoying the win.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation?
qa.a: Gurleen's point that Kishore never calls mistakes 'luck' showed the unfair double standard, and it made him stop and look at the drawing again.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he heard Kishore call the drawing 'nothing'?
qa.a: Papa might feel puzzled and a little sad, since he is proud enough to show the neighbours and wants Kishore to feel proud too.

grounding: Shows a teenager who wins a prize for a drawing and explains it away as luck and something anyone can do, until his sister points out the double standard.

passage: When I was fifteen, Lalit sir held up my charcoal sketch of a rain-soaked bus stop in front of the whole class and said, 'Siddharth, this is what I mean by mood.' Everyone turned to look at me. I remember my face going hot and my mouth saying, 'It was a fluke, sir. The charcoal smudged by accident.' It hadn't. I'd smudged it on purpose, after trying for two evenings. But admitting that felt dangerous, like claiming I was good, and I didn't think I was. Every compliment that year got the same treatment: luck, easy, anyone could. Every bad mark I kept like evidence. It took me a long time to notice the pattern. Now, when someone praises something I've made, I try to say just 'Thank you, I worked on it,' and let it sit there, even when it feels awkward.

qa.q: What was the charcoal sketch of?
qa.a: The sketch was of a rain-soaked bus stop.

qa.q: Why did admitting the smudge was on purpose feel dangerous to Siddharth?
qa.a: It would mean claiming to be good, which clashed with Siddharth's belief of not being good, so calling it a fluke kept that old self-view untouched.

qa.q: What does Siddharth do now with compliments, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Saying 'Thank you, I worked on it' lets the praise count and links it to real effort, instead of filing every good thing under luck.

qa.q: How might Lalit sir have felt when Siddharth called the sketch a fluke?
qa.a: Lalit sir may have felt a little puzzled or disappointed, since he was holding it up as a real example of mood, not an accident.

grounding: Shows someone looking back on a teenage habit of explaining away praise for a sketch as a fluke while keeping every bad mark as proof.

passage:
Art teacher's note, Class 9C, Thursday
Ritu's watercolour of the school garden was chosen for the district display today. When I told her in class, she said, 'Anyone could have done it, it's just a garden.' When a classmate said the sky was the best part, she said, 'The paper just soaked it up that way.' I've noticed she does this with every compliment, while she keeps a folder of her worst pieces 'to remember'. After class I asked her to tell me, step by step, how she painted the sky. She described three layers, waiting for each to dry, and lifting colour with a tissue. That isn't luck. I told her so, plainly, and asked her to write those three steps on the back of the painting before it goes to the district. She rolled her eyes, but she wrote them.
Zubin

qa.q: How many layers did Ritu describe for the sky?
qa.a: Ritu described three layers.

qa.q: Why might Ritu keep a folder of her worst pieces but wave away praise?
qa.a: Ritu seems to hold a low view of her own ability, so failures feel like the truth worth keeping, while praise feels like a mistake to explain away.

qa.q: Why was asking Ritu to describe how she painted the sky a smart move?
qa.a: Describing the three layers showed that the result came from skill and patience, making it harder to call it luck, and writing the steps down keeps that evidence.

qa.q: How might the classmate who praised the sky feel hearing 'The paper just soaked it up'?
qa.a: The classmate might feel brushed off, as if the compliment were wrong, and may be less likely to offer praise next time.

grounding: Shows an art teacher's note on a teenager who explains away every compliment on her painting as luck or anyone's work, while keeping her worst pieces.

passage:
Thursday

Today in art, Sir held up my drawing of the mango tree behind our school and said to the class, "Look at the light through the leaves. Mridul, how did you do this?"

Everyone looked at me. I said, "It was luck, sir. Anyone could do it." And I laughed so it would stop.

After class Sumit said, "Bro, you're the best at drawing in our whole class." I said, "No way, it's just that the tree is easy."

Here's the thing. It wasn't luck. I sat under that tree three evenings. I rubbed out the leaves maybe twenty times. But if I say that out loud, then I'd have to believe I'm actually good, and I'm not. I'm the average kid. That's what I am.

So the drawing doesn't count. Next time I'll probably mess up anyway, and then everyone will see.

Mridul

qa.q: How many evenings did Mridul sit under the mango tree?
qa.a: Three evenings.

qa.q: Why does Mridul say it was luck when he knows it wasn't?
qa.a: Admitting the effort worked would mean accepting he's good, which clashes with seeing himself as the average kid. Calling it luck keeps his old self-view safe.

qa.q: What small step could help Mridul let the praise count?
qa.a: Next time someone compliments him, he could just say "Thanks, it took three evenings." Naming his effort would let the good news actually land.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel when Mridul says the tree is just easy?
qa.a: Sumit might feel a little brushed off, since he meant the compliment. He may wonder why his friend can't accept being good at something.

grounding: A teenager praised for a drawing calls it luck and says anyone could do it, explaining away the good news so his negative self-view stays untouched.
